note: Of 51 implemented applications only one examined economic impact, which is a gap worth raising with any client business case.
title: Role of Artificial Intelligence Applications in Real-Life Clinical Practice: Systematic Review

reading.body:
Of 51 AI applications that reached real clinical use by 2020, exactly one measured financial impact. The evidence base for clinical AI is real but narrow.

The review covers implementations published from 2010 to 2020, found across medical databases, computer science venues, and trial registries. Thirteen were randomized controlled trials and eight used experimental designs. The applications cluster in screening, diagnosis, risk analysis, and treatment, with sepsis, breast cancer, diabetic eye disease, and colon polyps recurring. What the studies mostly measured was tool performance and effects on clinicians. What they mostly did not measure was whether patients did better, and almost never whether the money worked.

That gap matters for AI generally, not just medicine. A model that performs well in validation is not the same as a system that changes an outcome, and neither is the same as a system someone can justify paying for. The same sequence, capability first, then workflow, then cost, is what any deployment has to clear. Here, 50 of 51 implementations stopped before the last step.

What this does not tell you is why. The data records that only one study assessed financial effects, not whether the others found none, declined to look, or lacked the data to try. It also says nothing about compute, buildings, or power, which this review never examined. The 51 applications are a count of what was implemented and published, not a measure of what was built and abandoned.

explain_beginner: This review looked at artificial intelligence tools actually used in real patient care, not just tested in labs. The authors searched medical databases and other sources for studies from 2010 to 2020. They found 51 implemented applications. These tools helped with screening, diagnosis, risk checks, and treatment. Some common areas were sepsis, breast cancer, diabetic eye disease, and colon polyps. Many studies looked at how well the tools worked or how they affected doctors, but fewer looked at patient results. Only one looked at money impact. This matters because AI in medicine is promising but still early, and its real world value needs more proof.
explain_business: This review found 51 AI applications that reached real clinical use by 2020. They supported tasks such as screening, diagnosis, risk analysis, and treatment, often in areas like sepsis, breast cancer, diabetic eye disease, and colon polyps. Most evaluations looked at tool performance or effects on clinicians. Far fewer measured results for patients, and just one examined financial effects. For executives, that means clinical AI may offer promise, but the business case is usually unproven. A decision to invest should require local evidence on workflow fit, patient benefit, and cost or return, rather than relying only on technical validation or vendor claims.
explain_practitioner: The authors systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Central, CINAHL, computer science venues, and trial registries for real world clinical AI implementations published from January 2010 to May 2020. They included 51 studies. Thirteen used randomized controlled trials and eight used experimental designs. Applications covered screening, patient sorting, diagnosis, risk analysis, and treatment. Common conditions included sepsis, breast cancer, diabetic retinopathy, and polyp or adenoma. Evaluation focused mostly on how well tools performed and how they affected clinicians, with fewer assessing results for patients. Only one study assessed financial effects. The key result is that implementation evidence remains early and methodologically limited, so stronger evaluations are needed before broad adoption.
